title: Small Eyes, Big Problems: Nanophthalmos & Microphthalmos
summary: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into the spectrum of microphthalmic disorders. Distinguishing the structurally normal but miniaturized Nanophthalmos from the malformed Complex Microphthalmos is critical for preventing catastrophic surgical outcomes like uveal effusion.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Nanophthalmos is a specific subtype of 'simple microphthalmos' characterized by a small eye (Axial Length <20mm) with a structurally normal, though crowded, appearance. In contrast, Microphthalmos describes a small eye that often possesses internal structural anomalies (colobomas, persistent fetal vasculature, etc.).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Small corneal diameter (<10mm white-to-white)
Shallow anterior chamber (ACD <1.5mm common)
Relatively large lens (high lens-to-eye volume ratio)
Narrow or closed angles (high risk of ACG)
Fundus: Macular folds, crowded optic disc, tortuous vessels
Thick sclera (often >2.0 mm on ultrasound)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: The Surgical Nightmare
content: High risk of Spontaneous or Post-op Uveal Effusion
Expulsive Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage during intraocular surgery
Malignant Glaucoma (Ciliary Block) post-op
Non-rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Avoid sudden intraocular pressure drops during surgery

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Comprehensive Refraction: Confirm high hyperopia
2. A-Scan Biometry: Measure Axial Length (Gold Standard)
3. B-Scan Ultrasonography: Assess scleral thickness/choroidal status
4. Gonioscopy: Evaluate for angle closure or PAS
5. UBM (Ultrasound Biomicroscopy): Measure ACD and Ciliary Body anatomy
6. Fundus OCT: Check for foveal hypoplasia or macular folds

branches: Posterior Microphthalmos (Normal ant. seg, short AL)
High Hyperopia (Normal size eye, flat cornea/lens)

sections.title: Pre-Surgical Management Strategy
content: 1. Aggressive medical management of Glaucoma
2. Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) early if angle is narrow
3. Consider prophylactic Lamellar Sclerotomies (4 quadrants)
4. Pre-op systemics: Acetazolamide + Mannitol to soften eye
5. General anesthesia to ensure absolute control of venous pressure

sections.title: Surgical Technique: Phacoemulsification
content: Prefer micro-incisional approach (MICS)
Use OVD with high cohesive properties (Healon GV/5)
Perform small, centered capsulorhexis (risk of run-out)
Maintain deep AC: use automated infusion if possible
Consider IOL power: often requires 'piggyback' IOLs (e.g., +30 and +10)

content.explanation: N: Narrow angles/Near-sightedness (extreme hyperopia); A: Axial length (<20mm); N: No other malformations; O: Outflow issues (Uveal Effusion).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (Kanski Level)
content: The Lens-to-Eye Volume Ratio is 4-8x higher than normal in Nanophthalmos.
Uveal effusion syndrome occurs because the thick sclera acts like a 'noose' on vortex veins.
In Complex Microphthalmos, always check for systemic syndromes (e.g., Lenz, CHARGE, Walker-Warburg).
IOL calculation formulas: Haigis or Hoffer Q are generally more accurate for very short eyes.

sections.title: Recent Advances
content: Femtosecond laser-assisted sclerostomy (FLAS) for effusion management
AS-OCT guided angle assessment for surgical planning
Genetic counseling for MFRP-associated retinal dystrophies
Use of intrascleral IOL fixation (Yamane) in cases of zonular instability

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: Amblyopia management is paramount. Early full cycloplegic refraction and patching are required. Monitor for early-onset angle-closure glaucoma, which can occur as early as the second decade of life in nanophthalmic patients.
